q: It’s official! Telangana yaasa, which was for long oppressed and ridiculed, finally gets it due with the mainstream print, radio and TV using it to connect with its readers and audience.
2016 February 20, “Auv Malla! Telangana Dialect Triumphs Finally”, in The New Indian Express:
The actor, who took six months of prep to master the rural Telangana dialect of the 80s for Dorasaani, had to quickly unlearn the same and pick up the 'Guntur yaasa'.
2019 October 12, “Anand picks up Guntur slang to play a middle class Andhra abbayi next”, in Times of India:
Many have already described Palasa 1978 as the first ever Srikakulam based Telugu feature, with its yaasa, folk songs, places etc.
2020 March 15, “Dalitality in Palasa 1978: What Telugu Cinema Waited a Century to Say”, in The Citizen, archived from the original on 03 Dec 2020:

e: Borrowed from Pahari-Potwari یارا (yārā), vocative case of یار (yār), from Classical Persian یَار (yār). Doublet of yaar.
From Hindustani یار (yār) / यार (yār), from Classical Persian یار (yār).
q: ‘I'm going to make the most of my life now, yaar,’ he said.
1990, Hanif Kureishi, chapter 15, in The Buddha of Suburbia, London; Boston: Faber and Faber, →ISBN, page 222:
The SDP wanted a different political image from that portrayed in the BBC's Today in Parliament /Yesterday in Parliament reports — of juvenile yaa-boo exchanges on the floor of the House of Commons.
1982, Hugh Stephenson, Claret and chips: the rise of the SDP, page 10:

No! we hug each other, swooning and falling about with the ecstatically comforting knowledge that — yes! it's true! — those feminists have just gone too far. That we are, what we are! Men! Real Men! Yaa-boo!
1999, Jeff Raglus, Big Funky Action, page 220:

This is yaa-boo, in-yer-face, up-yours theatre, vaguely but crudely feminist; a Punch and Judy show with drab dialogue of naff lower-middle-class cliches. Ghastly sex scene, about as erotic as playing dominoes.
